title: The Informational Cost of Structure: Representational Complexity in Networked Dynamical Systems
authors: Cyril Rommens, Pietro Traversa, Guilherme Ferraz de Arruda, Yamir Moreno
abstract: How much information is required to represent a dynamical system in terms of an interaction structure and an evolution rule? We address this question using algorithmic information theory. We introduce Representational Complexity, the excess description length of a structure-plus-rule model relative to the shortest possible description of the dynamics itself. This intrinsic description defines a universal lower bound: no exact structural representation can be more concise. If arbitrary rules are allowed, graphs, hypergraphs, and other formalisms can all reach this bound by shifting information between structure and dynamics, so expressiveness alone cannot distinguish them. Meaningful differences arise only when scientific modeling restricts the admissible structures and rules. Within this setting, we identify conditions under which graph and hypergraph descriptions are informationally equivalent, and show how graph-preferred, hypergraph-preferred, and mixed regimes can emerge when those conditions are relaxed. Because Kolmogorov complexity is not computable, we complement the formal results with explicit description-length estimates. Our framework reframes the choice of network representation as a question of informational cost and mechanistic transparency rather than universal expressive power.
summary: This work introduces Representational Complexity to quantify the information overhead incurred when describing a dynamical system using specific structural models like graphs or hypergraphs. It shows that while expressive power is not enough, the choice of representation must minimize the total informational cost relative to the true dynamics. This framework suggests that genuinely many-body interactions require higher-order structures (hypergraphs) for an efficient and non-redundant description.
main_problem: The paper addresses determining the minimum informational cost required to represent a complex dynamical system using an explicit interaction structure and an evolution rule.
main_result: The choice of representation (e.g., graph vs. hypergraph) is not determined by mere expressive power, but rather by minimizing the total informational cost relative to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics itself.
method: It employs Algorithmic Information Theory, specifically using Representational Complexity ($	ext{RC}$), which measures the excess description length beyond the system's inherent Kolmogorov complexity $K(F)$.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on abstract networked dynamical systems modeled by finite Boolean maps ($F: \{0, 1\}^N 	o \{0, 1\}^N$), comparing representations based on pairwise interactions (graphs) versus higher-order interactions (hypergraphs).
key_observables: Representational Complexity ($	ext{RC}$), Algorithmic Mutual Information ($	ext{I}(D:S)$), and the difference in description length ($\Delta 	ext{RC}$) between structural representations.
important_parameters: The dimensionality of interactions ($k$), system size ($N$), and the specific constraints placed on admissible structures and rules (restricted vs. unrestricted settings).
main_assumptions: Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable, so results are complemented with explicit description-length estimates; comparisons assume fixed coding conventions for asymptotic analysis.
figures_summary: The notes detail several examples comparing costs: Group-Threshold dynamics favoring graphs if $k \ge 2$; SI-type rules showing external annotations add cost; and a direct comparison showing graph expansion of $k$-hyperedges is significantly more costly than the hypergraph representation for $k \ge 3$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes $	ext{RC}$ as the core metric, first proving its non-negativity ($	ext{RC} \ge 0$). It then contrasts the unrestricted setting (where all formalisms are equivalent) with restricted settings where structural constraints lead to measurable differences in informational cost between graph and hypergraph models.
why_interesting: While abstract, the framework provides a rigorous information-theoretic lens for model selection. In AMO physics, choosing between pairwise coupling terms (like simple nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians) versus higher-order interactions (e.g., three-body or Rydberg blockade effects) can be quantified by this informational cost.
